request: The Linda problem: is Linda more likely a bank teller, or a feminist bank teller? A two-voice dialogue quiz, with the nested sets drawn. #interactive #short
subtitle: Meet Linda, then pick the likelier story about her. See why most people choose wrong, and how two circles expose the conjunction fallacy.

spec.title: Linda: bank teller, or feminist bank teller?

sources.title: Extensional versus intuitive reasoning: the conjunction fallacy in probability judgment
sources.finding: about 85 % of respondents ranked 'bank teller and active in the feminist movement' as more probable than 'bank teller'

sources.title: Bully for Brontosaurus
sources.finding: Gould wrote that a homunculus in his head kept shouting that Linda can't just be a bank teller

elements.text: She can't just be a bank teller!

commands.speak: Here's a famous puzzle about a woman called Linda. Which story about her is more probable?
Linda is thirty-one, single, outspoken and very bright.
She studied philosophy. As a student she cared deeply about discrimination, and marched against nuclear weapons.

quiz.question: Which is more probable?
choices: Linda is a bank teller and a feminist
quiz.right: Bank teller. Every feminist bank teller is a bank teller too, so the pair can never be more likely.
quiz.wrong: Count what each answer needs to be true.

commands.speak: But she sounds exactly like a feminist!
She does. But draw it. Here are all the bank tellers in the world.
The feminist bank tellers are a group inside that one. However likely the story, the inner group can't be bigger.
Yet in Tversky and Kahneman's 1983 study, about eighty-five percent of people picked the second answer.
So more detail made the story feel more likely?
Exactly. They called it the conjunction fallacy: each added detail makes a story less likely, but more believable.
Even the biologist Stephen Jay Gould admitted a little voice in his head kept shouting: but she can't just be a bank teller!
